findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Revenue account reserves levels at start and end of 2025/26
findings.headline: Department of Community and Children's Services drew down its £1.846m reserve to bridge a structural funding gap, using one-off Home Office income pending permanent budget uplifts.
findings.detail: The DCCS reserve of £1.846m at the start of 2025/26 was fully drawn down by 31 March 2026. The paper explains this was one-off income from the Home Office relating to the Afghan Resettlement Scheme, held to bridge an acknowledged funding gap within DCCS until permanent budget uplifts were agreed for 2026/27.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know when a council has a structural funding gap and is using one-off money to bridge it, relying on promised permanent funding uplift.

findings.detail: A window replacement project significantly overran budget. The council notes this is due to project delivery delays, rescoping, and integration within a wider works programme. This is one of multiple fire safety and maintenance projects experiencing cost and schedule pressures.
findings.matters: Cost overruns on maintenance capital projects indicate either scope creep, delivery challenges, or underestimated complexity; multiple concurrent overruns suggest systemic project management pressure

findings.matters: Delays in occupying new housing stock delay revenue generation and indicate slippage on capital delivery, signalling project management or procurement challenges

findings.quote: Dwellings rental income had an adverse variance of £288,000, mainly due to lower than budgeted income expected from Black Raven Court and Bean Tree Court due to delays in the occupation of the new units.

This represents both an operational pressure (demand) and a contract execution issue (mobilisation cost).
findings.matters: Unexpected emergency repair demand and contract mobilisation costs indicate either housing stock condition challenges or contract management issues that could affect future budgets and service delivery
findings.figures: £786,000 overspend
findings.quote: Breakdown and Emergency Repair costs were overspent by £786,000. The increased expenditure was driven by increased demand for breakdown and emergency repairs and an additional contractual one-off contract cost associated with the mobilisation of the Chigwell R&M contract.

Costs cover interim repair works, condition surveys, and professional fees to address water ingress. The framing as interim measures indicates an ongoing capital problem requiring future remediation.
findings.matters: Significant unplanned maintenance spend signals infrastructure condition risk; ongoing remediation suggests either deferred maintenance or unexpected asset deterioration
findings.figures: £156,000 adverse variance in Surveyor R&M budget
findings.quote: The adverse v ariance within Surveyor Repairs and Maintenance Cyclical Works is primarily due to expenditure incurred in relation to Golden Lane Leisure Centre, including interim repair works, condition surveys and associated professional fees required to address water ingress and support the development of longer-term remedial solutions.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care demand-led overspend of £278,000 with structural volatility acknowledged

findings.headline: City Fund committed to significant HRA capital funding over 10 years, constraining financial flexibility
findings.detail: City Fund has made a long-term commitment to support Housing Revenue Account (HRA) capital expenditure to improve the housing stock. The document states financial resources 'will need to be continually managed to ensure sustainability is a priority'. This multi-year commitment locks in future expenditure.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy Statement and Annual Investment Strategy (relating to Treasury Management) 2026/27
findings.headline: Inflation erosion of £1.08bn in long-term cash reserves flagged as 'one of the most acute challenges'
findings.detail: As at 31 December 2025, the Corporation holds £1,080.9m in cash balances, primarily in money market funds and fixed income. Cash is expected to decline as the capital programme spends, but core balances are expected to persist for the next 10 years. The document explicitly identifies preventing real value erosion from inflation as a major strategic challenge.
findings.matters: A large council holding significant reserves over a decade faces material real-value erosion risk; this is a governance issue around adequacy of returns and whether the council is properly protecting real asset value.
findings.figures: £1,080.9m (as at 31 December 2025); core cash expected to persist for next 10 years
findings.quote: One of the most acute challenges within the treasury management strategy is preventing the gradual erosion of the real value of these long-term cash balances from the effects of inflation.

findings.headline: Cautious interest rate strategy with contingency to accelerate external borrowing if rates spike sharply.
findings.detail: The strategy states 'caution will be adopted with the 2026/27 treasury operations' and commits to monitor for significant risks. If forecasted rate falls do not materialise and there is 'a much sharper RISE in long and short term rates' (e.g. from US or UK central bank decisions), the Chamberlain will 'draw fixed rate funding whilst interest rates are lower than they are projected to be in the next few years.' This signals the council may suddenly move from under-borrowed to externally borrowed if economic conditions shift.
findings.matters: The council's current zero-borrowing stance is conditional on stable or falling rates. A sharp rate rise could trigger unplanned external borrowing, increasing the debt burden rapidly.
findings.figures: Bank Rate forecast 3.75% (Mar 2026) declining to 3.25% (Dec 2026); PWLB 5-year 4.60% to 4.10%
findings.quote: if it was felt that there was a significant risk of a much sharper RISE in long and short term rates than that currently forecast, perhaps arising from an increase in central rates in the USA and UK, an increase in world economic activity, or a sudden increase in inflation risks, then the portfolio position will be re-appraised. Most likely, fixed rate funding will be drawn whilst interest rates are lower than they are projected to be in the next few years.

findings.headline: Investment balances forecast to decline from current £1.08bn to minimum floor of £610m over medium term.
findings.detail: The council projects investment balances will decline 'over the next few years as the capital programme is progressed' but 'remain above/at a minimum constant level of £610m'. This 44% reduction in liquid resources is consistent with the reserve-funded capital spending noted above. The council is committed to maintaining this £610m floor.
findings.matters: The declining liquidity profile constrains the council's ability to absorb shocks or unexpected capital needs and limits additional borrowing capacity as reserves deplete.
findings.figures: £1,080.9m current investment balances (31 December 2025); £610m minimum projected level
findings.quote: total investment balances within the treasury investment portfolio are expected to decline over the next few years as the capital programme is progressed but to remain above/at a minimum constant level of £610m

findings.headline: Fair value volatility in £324.9m pooled bond fund holdings (30% of portfolio) managed by hedging through a ringfenced IFRS 9 reserve.
findings.detail: The council holds £324.9m in ultra-short and short-dated bond funds through external managers. The document signals concern about fair value volatility by stating 'To mitigate against any reduction in value, a ringfenced IFRS9 reserve will be created in 2024/25.' This reserve will absorb unrealised losses to prevent them hitting the revenue account. The statutory override protecting these holdings expires 31 March 2029.
findings.matters: This indicates the council acknowledges material valuation risk in its investment portfolio. Creation of a hedging reserve suggests past or expected losses. When the override expires in 2029, fair value volatility will hit revenue unless reserves are released.
findings.figures: £324.9m in bond funds as at 31 December 2025; £600.9m total external fund management
findings.quote: To mitigate against any reduction in value, a ringfenced IFRS9 reserve will be created in 2024/25 with funding from the overachievement of investment income

findings.headline: City's Estate £450m external debt to be reduced gradually over time through property disposals rather than cash reserves.
findings.detail: City's Estate carries £450m fixed-rate market debt (£250m from 2019/20, £200m from 2021/22). Rather than use its cash to pay this down, the council commits to 'liquidation of financial investments and investment property disposals' as the mechanism for debt reduction. This places the debt repayment strategy outside treasury control and makes it dependent on property market conditions.
findings.matters: The repayment pathway for this debt is contingent on property sales, not budgeted revenue or cash reserves. Market downturns would delay debt reduction and extend the council's leverage ratio.
findings.figures: £450m total outstanding external borrowing; £250m issued 2019/20 at fixed rate; £200m issued 2021/22 at fixed rate
findings.quote: A debt financing strategy will be established to ensure borrowing for City's Estate is reduced gradually over time

findings.headline: Capital programme over five years financed primarily from capital reserves, not external borrowing, totalling £924m drawdown.
findings.detail: The City Fund's capital programme for 2026/27 of £450.5m is financed £338.4m from capital reserves (75%), £99.0m from grants, and only £13.1m from revenue. Across 2025/26–2029/30, capital reserves are consumed at £924.1m total. The council maintains a zero external borrowing position by using internal cash resources, which over time increases its reliance on property disposals and reserve depletion.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's capital programme is self-funding or depleting its financial cushion. Heavy reliance on reserve drawdown limits future flexibility and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: £450.5m capital expenditure 2026/27; £338.4m from capital reserves; £924.1m total capital reserves consumed 2025/26–2029/30; City Fund has £0 external debt
findings.quote: All projected capital expenditure in 2026/27 will be financed from revenue contributions, earmarked reserves, and supported by the liquidation of financial investments and additional property disposals.

findings.committee: City of London Police Authority Board
findings.headline: The 2026/27 budget relies on £7.2m of budget mitigations, including an unidentified £587k, to balance.
findings.detail: The budget includes: Natural Vacancy Factor (civilian staff) £0.982m; Action Fraud exceptional cost release £4.0m; increased recovery of overhead from funded work £1.588m; Report Fraud new delivery approach £587k. Of these, the £587k is explicitly unidentified and the natural vacancy factor is a risky assumption that depends on timing of recruitment and leavers.
findings.matters: The budget balance depends on achieving all of these mitigations. If any fail—if the Action Fraud cost release doesn't materialise, if the overhead recovery proves optimistic, or if the £587k cannot be identified—the budget will not balance. These are not efficiency gains; they are gap-filling.
findings.figures: Total budget mitigations £7.157m; comprising: Natural Vacancy £0.982m, Action Fraud release £4.0m, overhead recovery £1.588m, unidentified £587k

findings.committee: City of London Police Authority Board
findings.headline: Proceeds of Crime Act reserve is now being drawn down to fund routine operational costs of asset recovery teams, not exceptional items.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes a planned £1.895m release from the POCA reserve to fund the net operating costs of the Asset Recovery and Civil Recovery Teams. This practice began in 2023/24 as a temporary mitigation due to budgetary pressures. The reserve is now forecast to fall from £3.1m at March 2026 to £1.7m at March 2027, and to £0.1m by March 2028 at current drawdown rates.
findings.matters: The Force is treating reserve balances as a funding source for recurring operational costs rather than for emergencies or exceptional items. At current drawdown rates, this reserve will be exhausted within three years, eliminating a source of resilience.
findings.figures: POCA reserve drawdown 2026/27 £1.895m; forecast balance March 2026 £3.1m; forecast balance March 2027 £1.7m; forecast balance March 2028 £0.1m (implied)

findings.committee: City of London Police Authority Board
findings.headline: Borrowing expected to increase from £0.9m to £7.5m by March 2026, with potential to reach £17.5m if capital projects require funding.
findings.detail: The Force has planned borrowing of £6.6m from an internal City Corporation loan facility to fund its share of FCCRAS capital costs. The paper notes: 'While the expectation is that CoLP's project programme priorities will normally be managed within the £5m DRF envelope, there may be exceptional circumstances where recourse to the internal loan facility may be necessary and appropriate. Such circumstances may include funding for the new firing range, if a capital partnership does not materialise. Should this prove to be the case, total borrowing could potentially increase up to circa £17.5m.'
findings.matters: The Force's borrowing is forecast to double from current levels and could potentially treble if additional capital projects require funding. This represents a material liability increase that is contingent on unresolved capital partnership negotiations.
findings.figures: Accrued borrowing April 2025 £0.9m; forecast March 2026 £7.5m; potential 2026/27 total £17.5m; internal loan facility being drawn
findings.quote: Should this prove to be the case, total borrowing could potentially increase up to circa £17.5m in 2026/27.

findings.committee: City of London Police Authority Board
findings.headline: Comprehensive Spending Review funding expected to be front-loaded did not materialise; this increases risk to budgets in 2027/28 and 2028/29.
findings.detail: The Force was budgeted on the assumption that the three-year CSR (£2bn nationally, 11% increase over three years 2026/27 to 2028/29) would be front-loaded, with higher funding in year one falling back in years two and three. The settlement shows this will not happen: 'Based on the current settlement this will now not be the case, which may increase the risk to balancing budgets in 27/28 and 28/29.'
findings.matters: The Force's medium-term financial plan was built on an assumption about how government funding would be distributed. That assumption has proven wrong. The Force will face significant pressure to balance budgets in the following two years.
findings.figures: Multi-year CSR £2bn nationally (11% over three years); funding uplift 2026/27 £4.0m (4.3%); 2026/27 increase £2.8m below previous MTFP forecast
findings.quote: Based on the current settlement this will now not be the case, which may increase the risk to balancing budgets in 27/28 and 28/29.

findings.committee: City of London Police Authority Board
findings.headline: FCCRAS/Report Fraud service has a residual £587k funding gap that is included as an unidentified saving in the 2026/27 budget.
findings.detail: The revised Full Business Case for FCCRAS identified a £5m pa funding gap. The Home Office approved only a £3-4m pa funding increase. The Force is now expected to increase its contribution from £1.5m to £2.5m pa. Even after this, 'there remains a residual gap of £587k, which has been included at this stage as an unidentified saving in the 2026/27 budget.' This is a live service delivery risk baked into the budget.
findings.matters: The Force has a critical national function (fraud, economic and cybercrime) with a funding gap. The £587k is listed as unidentified, meaning there is no firm plan for how to deliver it. The paper hopes 'opportunities for higher contributions for partner agencies and scope of recharging will also help bridge this gap.'
findings.figures: FCCRAS funding gap £5m pa; Home Office increase £3-4m; CoLP contribution increase £1m; residual gap £587k included as unidentified saving
findings.quote: there remains a residual gap of £587k, which has been included at this stage as an unidentified saving in the 2026/27 budget

findings.committee: City of London Police Authority Board
findings.headline: Staff pay budget for 2026/27 does not include costs from the Ambition 25 pay and grading review; costs are unquantified but known to be incoming.
findings.detail: The budget assumes 3.0% pay inflation for staff but the paper states: 'Critically, the staff pay assumption does not include a provision for the impact of the organisational pay and grading review known as Ambition 25. A funding solution will be required for any additional future staff pay costs once quantified.' This is a known cost that is not yet reflected in the budget.
findings.matters: The budget excludes a known future cost. Once Ambition 25 is costed, the Force will need to find additional funding mid-year or make cuts elsewhere. Staff pay is the largest budget item (£48.8m for police staff alone).
findings.figures: Staff pay budget 2026/27 £48.8m (3.0% assumption); Ambition 25 costs not yet quantified; pay risk £0.3m per 1% above assumption
findings.quote: Critically, the staff pay assumption does not include a provision for the impact of the organisational pay and grading review known as Ambition 25. A funding solution will be required for any additional future staff pay costs once quantified.

findings.committee: City of London Police Authority Board
findings.headline: Structural cost pressures of £10.5m in 2026/27 are only partly funded; the problem accelerates to £24.8m by 2029/30.
findings.detail: The Force faces major new pressures from higher inflation, pay awards, and increasing operational demands. These total £10.5m in the coming year and rise to £24.8m by 2029/30. The available new funding increase is only £2.8m. The paper notes: 'Beyond 2026/27...balancing the MTFP will require a strong drive on productivity and the realisation of cashable efficiencies from 2027/28.' This is a structural mismatch.
findings.matters: The Force faces a growing funding gap over the medium term that cannot be addressed through existing budget assumptions. This creates pressure to either deliver unrealistic efficiency gains, access additional borrowing, or reduce services.
findings.figures: Cost pressures £10.5m in 2026/27, rising to £24.8m in 2029/30; available new funding increase £2.8m; cumulative savings to date £20m
findings.quote: CoLP continues to experience a range of major new pressures including higher inflation, pay awards and increasing operational demands all of which present a risk to Police Finances – these are estimated to be £10.5m in 2026/27 rising to £24.8m in 29/30.

findings.committee: City of London Police Authority Board
findings.headline: Provisional settlement announced without the usual grant breakdown, creating planning uncertainties until end January 2026.
findings.detail: The Home Office issued only an aggregate funding figure of £96.7m on 18 December 2025, without the usual breakdown of individual grant elements. The paper warns: 'there is a potential risk of further ringfencing and associated delivery costs until the final settlement is confirmed.' £1.2m of the expected NLF grant funding has not yet been formally confirmed by the Home Office.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's budget is founded on confirmed funding or assumptions that could change materially in January 2026, just one month before the financial year starts.
findings.figures: £96.7m core grant settlement (vs usual full breakdown); £37.5m of £64.3m anticipated NLF funding formally confirmed; final settlement not expected until end January 2026
findings.quote: Given the current lack of information, for example, there is a potential risk of further ringfencing and associated delivery costs until the final settlement is confirmed.

findings.committee: City of London Police Authority Board
findings.paper_title: Report of action taken - Revenue Budget and Project Fund for 2026/27
findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cityoflondon.gov.uk/documents/s229755/Report of Action Taken - 26 27 Revenue and Budget setting.pdf
findings.headline: National Lead Force funding for 2026/27 remained unconfirmed at the point the budget was approved.
findings.detail: The Resource and Estates Committee meeting on 10 February 2026 endorsed the budget but acknowledged financial risks, specifically noting that funding for the National Lead Force was still to be confirmed for 2026/27. This represents income uncertainty at the point of budget approval.
findings.matters: Unconfirmed income sources create cash-flow risk and could force mid-year budget reductions or require reserve drawdown if the funding does not materialise.
findings.quote: This includes the late confirmation on funding for the National Lead Force, was still to be confirmed for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Dispersed estate structure and decades of underinvestment create inherent cost disadvantages
findings.detail: The council identifies structural pressures beyond national issues: a small dispersed estate spread across six London boroughs complicating service delivery, decades of underinvestment creating a repair backlog, and contractor administration causing delays and cost increases. These structural constraints limit the council's ability to achieve economies of scale and full HRA sustainability.
findings.matters: The structural disadvantages (dispersed estate, deferred maintenance backlog, scale constraints) suggest inherent challenges in achieving HRA financial sustainability and may require long-term service changes or general fund cross-subsidy
findings.figures: 1,921 rented homes (c.20% of London borough average of 15,000–16,000 units); dispersed across six boroughs
findings.quote: A small, dispersed Estate whose geographic spread complicates centralised service delivery and increases operational costs. This dispersed and relatively small stock size poses unique challenges, including higher per-unit costs and difficulties achieving economies of scale compared to other local authorities.

findings.headline: New-builds remain unoccupied; rental income delayed into next year
findings.detail: Black Raven Court was forecast to generate full-year rental income but remains unoccupied with handover now delayed until January 2026. This delays income and contributes to an £208k shortfall in dwelling rent compared to budget.
findings.matters: Income delays worsen cash flow during a period of structural HRA pressure; and repeated delays suggest either project delivery risk or market constraints
findings.figures: Dwelling rent shortfall: £208k; Black Raven Court delayed from 52-week to ~12-week income in 2025/26
findings.quote: Estimates for Black Raven Court had been profiled for the full 52-week period of the 2025–26 financial year. However, due to ongoing delays in the building handover process, it remains unoccupied and, and will likely not be occupied until January 2026.

findings.headline: £1.1m of deficit improvement depends on auditor agreement to capitalize repair costs
findings.detail: The reduction from £1.3m overspend to £50k deficit relies heavily on 'identified capitalisations that will need to be agreed with auditors.' The council notes the treatment 'will also need to be reviewed and validated by our auditors.' If auditors disallow the capitalization, the deficit balloons back up.
findings.matters: The council's reported year-end position is contingent on accounting treatment not yet validated; audit disagreement would materially worsen finances and expose previously-hidden losses
findings.figures: £1.1m identified for capitalization; total P6-to-latest improvement: £1.25m
findings.quote: To ensure this method withstands auditor scrutiny, it will also need to be reviewed and validated by our auditors.

findings.headline: Current-year deficit is being funded by drawing down already-thin reserves
findings.detail: The £1.3m overspend at Period 6 has been reduced to a £50k deficit by the latest forecast, but this 'improved' position is still being funded from brought-forward reserves. Even with the best-case scenario, the account is not self-balancing; it is consuming reserves annually.
findings.matters: Year-on-year reserve drawdown is unsustainable; combined with low absolute reserve levels, this pattern signals structural imbalance in the HRA
findings.figures: P6: £1.3m overspend; Latest: £50k deficit; reserves: £324k
findings.quote: This adverse position has been reduced to a £0.05m deficit in the latest forecast with this small deficit being funded from brought forward reserves.

findings.headline: Revenue reserves are dangerously low; any overspend would breach statutory duties
findings.detail: Brought-forward reserves stand at only £324k on an HRA with £18m+ in net income. The report explicitly warns that given low reserve levels, any in-year overspend will breach the statutory requirement to retain a positive overall HRA balance. This exposes the council to a governance failure.
findings.matters: A statutory breach in housing finances would signal serious control weakness and is precisely the kind of red flag lenders monitor for solvency risk
findings.figures: £324k carried forward reserves; initial P6 forecast was £1.3m overspend
findings.quote: Low levels of revenue reserves mean that any in year budget overspend is likely to lead to a breach of statutory responsibilities to retain a positive balance on overall HRA funds.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account (HRA) and Capital Budgets 2026/27
findings.headline: Rent income dependent on aggressive 4.8% increases to support cost pressures
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget relies on rent income growth of £1,962k from a 4.8% increase (CPI + 1%) plus new build contributions. This growth must fund simultaneous cost pressures: £669k in employee cost inflation, £138k in higher energy costs, and £653k in increased technical services recharges for the capital programme.
findings.matters: The budget is structurally dependent on sustained rent growth. Limited headroom means the account has reduced resilience to economic shocks or cost overruns.
findings.figures: rent increase £1,962k (4.8% uplift); employee costs +£669k; energy costs +£138k; technical services +£653k
findings.quote: The Rent Increase of £1,962m reflects the CPI + 1% (total 4.8%) uplift which has been applied to existing dwellings for 2026/27. Further increases in rent income is attributed to the expected additional income in year from the 66 new flats at Black Raven Court, as well as the budgeted income for the 110 new flats at Sydenham Hill and the 91 new flats at York Way.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account (HRA) and Capital Budgets 2026/27
findings.headline: Revenue reserves tight until income from three new housing developments starts
findings.detail: The council explicitly describes its General Housing Revenue Reserve position as 'tight in the short term' with only £325k carried forward to 2026/27. Improvement to £1.3m reserves depends on delayed income from three new-build schemes. These schemes have already slipped once (described as 'delayed income').
findings.matters: A ring-fenced account with minimal reserves has no buffer for cost overruns or further timing delays. If the Black Raven Court, Sydenham Hill or York Way schemes slip again, the HRA faces immediate funding pressure.
findings.figures: General Housing Revenue Reserve £325k carried forward 2025/26; expected £1,319k 2026/27; new units: 66 + 110 + 91 = 267 units
findings.quote: However, the Revenue Reserve position remains tight in the short term but delayed income from new build projects at Black Raven Court, Sydenham Hill and York Way is expected to start in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Housing Revenue Account (HRA) and Capital Budgets 2026/27
findings.headline: £2.6m potential health & safety compliance costs not budgeted or funded
findings.detail: The revenue budget excludes potential costs up to £2.6m for health & safety staffing and repairs to meet new legal requirements. Funding is conditional on MHCLG agreeing to capitalise the costs or alternative funding arrangements being found.
findings.matters: An unfunded contingent liability of this size represents a material risk to the HRA's financial position if the council must fund these costs from existing resources.
findings.figures: up to £2.6m
findings.quote: The budget does not include funding for potential new health & safety staffing and repairs costs to comply with new legal requirements of up to £2.6m. These are subject to a capitalisation determination agreement from MHLGG or alternative funding arrangements.

findings.matters: Additional staffing to manage homelessness and housing services indicates the council is responding to service demand, but the growth in staffing costs (from £8.544m to £9.921m, a 16.1% increase) outpaces inflation provision, suggesting structural demand pressures.
findings.figures: 126 to 134 FTEs (8 additional posts, 6.3% increase); staff costs increasing from £8.544m to £9.921m (16.1% increase)

findings.paper_title: Departmental Budget Estimates 2026/27 - Community and Children's Services excluding Housing Revenue Account (HRA)
findings.headline: Asylum seekers service faces demand pressure from demographic cliff as young people age out of Home Office funding
findings.detail: The council has identified £52,000 of savings pressures within the asylum seekers service. The root cause is that young people who are asylum seekers age from 17 to 18, after which the Home Office provides little or no funding. The council must then fund care from 18 onwards.
findings.matters: This represents a predictable structural demand cliff where Home Office funding ends and council funding must begin, creating a defined but growing financial exposure.
findings.figures: £52,000 savings requirement within asylum seekers service budget
findings.quote: These pressures are arising from the number of individuals turning 18, who  then attract little or no funding from the Home Office.

findings.headline: Budget includes £450,000 of unidentified savings that have not yet been specified
findings.detail: The 2026/27 revenue budget is constructed with £450,000 of 'unidentified savings' included within the central risk budget. This comprises £398,000 for homelessness and temporary accommodation costs and £52,000 for the asylum seekers service. findings.quote: an unidentified savings requirement of £450,000 has been included within central risk,  comprising £3 98,000 for homelessness  and temporary accommodation costs  and £52 ,000 for the asylum seekers service.

findings.quote: The Housing Benefit Administration central risk budget  for 2026/27  includes a £300,000 transfer from the DCCS reserves to cover the shortfall between housing benefits payments for temporary accommodations and the amounts reimbursed by the Department for Work and Pensions.

findings.headline: Council will fund growing capital programme from reserve depletion via internal borrowing, deliberately avoiding external debt to prevent revenue pressure from debt service costs
findings.detail: City Fund holds £1,038.7m of cash as at 30 September 2025 but faces growing capital financing requirements in years ahead. The council plans to fund this through internal borrowing—spending from existing reserves—explicitly to avoid 'revenue pressures in the immediate term' that external debt service would create. Officers acknowledge that 'cash balances are expected to reduce meaningfully over the medium term as spending on the capital programme increases,' meaning this strategy will progressively exhaust reserves.
findings.matters: Lenders need to forecast when reserves will be depleted and external borrowing will become necessary, and what future debt service costs will be. Finance directors need to model the medium-term capital programme and its impact on cash flow and revenue budgets.
findings.figures: £1,038.7m cash at 30 September 2025; growing capital financing requirement forecast; funding via internal borrowing (reserve spend) not external debt
findings.quote: Although the City Fund is forecast to have a growing capital financing requirement forecast in the years ahead, it expects to be able to fund this in the short term via internal borrowing.

findings.committee: City of London Police Authority Board
findings.headline: Recruitment difficulties and increased staff turnover create risk of higher future hiring costs or service degradation
findings.detail: Applications per campaign dropped from average 19 to 11 in the latest period; 6 campaigns received no applications; officer leaver rate doubled from 1% to 2% and staff turnover rose from 1.7% to 2.3%. This combination suggests difficulty retaining staff and recruiting replacements, which could force higher wage offers or increased reliance on agency staff.
findings.matters: If the Police Authority cannot fill roles at advertised rates, it may face pressure to offer higher pay to compete, or to fund agency staff at premium rates, both of which would strain the already-tight budget
findings.figures: Officer leaver rate: 1% to 2% (Q1 to Q2); Staff turnover: 1.7% to 2.3%; Applications per campaign: 19 average down to 11; 6 campaigns with zero applications
findings.quote: On average, 11 applications were received per campaign (previous average of 19 applications per campaign)... The officer leaver rate increased from 1% in June 2025 to 2% in September 2025, staff leavers has increased from 1.7% to 2.3%

findings.matters: The council's finance director needs to reserve budget across the medium-term plan for these 156 new positions; this is a committed future spend that will impact council resources

findings.quote: Current growth forecasts suggest funding for up to 77 staff and officer roles is being sought with recruitment planned up to 2027/28; additionally, O3C is estimated to grow by 79 posts across officers and staff to 2027/28

findings.committee: City of London Police Authority Board

findings.figures: £122.4m forecast outturn (breakeven); Q1 forecast was £0.9m overspend; expected to remain within 1% of breakeven

findings.headline: Paper identifies further investment required for aging stock and new compliance standards but does not quantify the cost.
findings.detail: The strategy states "Further investment required to address ageing stock and compliance with new standards" but provides no figures. The only spend figures given are current annual spend (£4.3M repairs, £1M servicing/safety). The full extent of future capital obligations remains undefined pending the 2026 survey completion.
findings.matters: A lender must understand forward-looking capital requirements to assess the council's ability to maintain its housing estate and comply with regulatory standards without accessing additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Annual spend: £4.3M day-to-day repairs and minor works; £1M servicing and safety checks
findings.quote: Investment Needs: Further investment required to address ageing stock and compliance with new standards.

findings.headline: Housing portfolio is being managed on asset data from 2018, with new condition surveys not expected until 2026.
findings.detail: The authority is operating an interim asset management strategy based on eight-year-old stock condition data, professional judgment, and feedback, explicitly because a full current survey programme will not complete until 2026. The paper acknowledges this creates incompleteness that may require priorities to shift once new data arrives.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that an authority has current visibility of maintenance needs across a £multi-million housing portfolio. Planning on decade-old data creates risk of unidentified capital requirements.
findings.figures: 1,923 social rented homes and 971 leasehold homes; last comprehensive survey undertaken in 2018; new survey completion targeted for 2026

A new programme of surveys has commenced with pilot surveys being undertaken and completion targeted for 2026. findings.headline: Social care and asylum budgets explicitly noted as highly volatile, with small client-number changes creating major forecast swings
findings.detail: The report warns that both social care and asylum budgets are very volatile and responsive to small demographic shifts. Asylum Seekers is currently £106,000 overspent; Adult Social Care £77,000; Older People's £108,000, with impacts dependent on client movements and service demand.
findings.matters: Volatile budgets create forecasting risk and unpredictability; client-driven services can diverge sharply from forecast mid-year, complicating financial management on tight margins
findings.figures: Asylum Seekers £106,000 overspend (may improve with care leaver relocations); Adult Social Care £77,000 overspend; Older People £108,000 overspend
findings.quote: In general, it should be noted that both the social care and asylum budgets are very volatile and a small change in client numbers has a major effect on the eventual full year outturn.

findings.detail: The council awards housing benefits for temporary accommodations but receives insufficient reimbursement from DWP, creating a material shortfall. Some accommodations are running over their planned limits, and shortage of temporary accommodation at reasonable prices has worsened the gap between what the council pays and what it recovers.
findings.matters: This is material unfunded pressure the council must absorb mid-year, driven by market forces largely outside its control, and indicates ongoing structural cost pressures in temporary accommodation
findings.figures: £633,000 overspend on a £67,000 original budget; total Housing Benefit forecast moved to £700,000 deficit
findings.quote: Housing Benefit Administration central risk budget is projecting an estimated overspend of £633 ,000. This is largely attributable to a shortfall between housing benefits awarded for temporary accommodations and payments made by the Department for Work and Pensions. Some of the accommodations are over their limit and the shortage of temporary accommodation at reasonable prices led to the increased shortfall in this area.

findings.headline: Inflation contingency and 2% cost uplift being maintained, with CPI at 3.5% as of April 2025, creating ongoing budget pressure.
findings.detail: Inflation rates are being monitored quarterly. The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rose by 3.5% in the 12 months to April 2025, up from 2.6% in the 12 months to March. An inflation contingency is being maintained in 2025/26 through carried forward from 2024/25 underspends, plus a net 2% inflation uplift has been approved in local risk budgets.
findings.matters: Persistent inflation above the Bank of England target is eroding the value of the inflation contingency and creating a structural gap between budget assumptions and actual cost pressures, which must be closed through service cuts or income.
findings.figures: CPI 3.5% (12 months to April 2025); 2% inflation uplift approved for 2025/26 budgets
findings.quote: The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) rose by 3.5% in the 12 months to April 2025, up from 2.6% in the 12 months to March.

findings.headline: Cyclical Works Programme funding confirmed at £133m over five years, reducing property maintenance backlog risk.
findings.detail: In March 2024, the Court of Common Council agreed £133m funding to be delivered over five years for the Cyclical Works Programme. The delivery team was established in late 2024 and works have commenced. The risk impact scoring has reduced 'to reflect the agreement of funding of CWP.'
findings.matters: A significant aging property estate with deferred maintenance is a long-term liability and operational cost driver. Securing ringfenced funding for cyclical maintenance is a positive indicator of capital discipline.
findings.figures: £133m funding agreed for Cyclical Works Programme over five years; delivery commenced late 2024
findings.quote: In March 2024 the Court of Common Council agreed £133m funding to be delivered over five years to support the Cyclical Works Programme (CWP). The scoring on the impact of this risk has reduced from initial scoring to reflect the agreement of funding of CWP.

findings.headline: Major capital schemes carry significant funding and cost risks, particularly for SSD/FPEP projects, despite current budget forecasts.
findings.detail: The capital programme risk notes that while 'All projects are currently forecast to be completed within budget, although there are quite significant risks to funding and costs, which will continue to be reviewed, particularly relating to SSD/FPEP.' A portfolio management model is being introduced to better prioritise projects against strategic objectives. The Markets Co-location Programme was cancelled, and a new Markets Programme initiated.
findings.matters: Significant risks to major project funding and costs indicate potential for capital overruns or delay, which would increase debt pressure and reduce asset realisation proceeds needed to fund operating deficits.
findings.figures: SSD/FPEP projects flagged as carrying significant risks; Markets programme cancelled and restarted
findings.quote: All projects are currently forecast to be completed within budget, although there are quite significant risks to funding and costs, which will continue to be reviewed, particularly relating to SSD/FPEP.

findings.headline: City's Estate fund forecasts £395m cumulative deficit over five-year plan, though balance sheet modelling indicates this is manageable if investment strategy succeeds.
findings.detail: The City's Estate (non-City Fund properties) is producing annual operating deficits across the five-year plan. The revised cumulative deficit is £395m. However, the report notes that 'Balance sheet modelling indicates this is manageable in the medium term' and expects a transition into surplus in 15 years if the investment strategy is implemented. A key caveat: 'failure to implement the investment strategy will compromise the recovery of City's Estate's I&E position.'
findings.matters: A £395m cumulative deficit on one fund indicates significant structural imbalance. While balance sheet capacity currently exists, this signals dependence on property asset strategy working and carries refinancing risk if asset values or investment returns disappoint.
findings.figures: £395m cumulative deficit forecast; recovery to surplus projected in 15 years
findings.quote: the revised cumulative deficit is forecast to be £395m in additional to the financial gain already modelled. Balance sheet modelling indicates this is manageable in the medium term... failure to implement the investment strategy will compromise the recovery of City's Estate's I&E position.

findings.headline: City Fund enters deficit from 2026/27 onwards, requiring radical decisions to bring down annual operating deficit.
findings.detail: The 2025/26 budget and medium term financial plan confirms a shift from the business rates reset. The council will move into deficit position from 2026/27 onwards. The report states that 'Radical decisions are now needed on how best to bring down the annual operating deficit, over and above those already identified (income generation, operational property review, investment property review), including major changes or stoppages to existing services provision and/or reduction in grants.'
findings.matters: This is the core financial sustainability issue: a statutory body moving into structural deficit requires either major service cuts, income increases, or reserve drawdown, all of which affect lender confidence and the council's financial resilience.
findings.figures: City Fund moves into deficit from 2026/27 onwards
findings.quote: City Fund moves into deficit position from 2026/27 onwards. Radical decisions are now needed on how best to bring down the annual operating deficit, over and above those already identified

findings.headline: Audit not yet complete; significant IT control breach over access to production diagnostics tools.
findings.detail: The auditor identified that 2 users were granted access to diagnostic tools within the Oracle EBS production environment, breaching segregation of duties and access control protocols. This was factored into enhanced testing of unusual journals by those users. The auditor has not concluded the audit and continues to await responses on queries about journals, collection fund debtors, payroll, assets under construction, and other items.
findings.matters: IT access controls protect against fraud, data theft, and unauthorized financial transactions. Segregation of duties is a foundational control. An unresolved multi-year control gap around small-value journal approvals creates ongoing risk of misstatement, particularly management override.
findings.figures: 2 users with inappropriate access; journals below £100k threshold lack approval control

findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cityoflondon.gov.uk/documents/s223173/City of London Corporation - City Fund Audit Findings Report 2024-25.pdf
findings.headline: Asset classification errors across £38.4m requiring prior period adjustments.
findings.detail: Audit testing identified material misclassification of assets under construction (AUC). Management had classified all 2024-25 AUC additions of £153.2m solely as PPE, but some should have been classified as investment property under development or intangible assets. Adjustments totalled £19.2m of PPE at year-end, with £13m reclassified to investment properties under development and £6.2m to intangible assets, requiring prior period adjustments.
findings.matters: Asset classification affects depreciation, impairment testing, and disclosure requirements. Whilst these adjustments do not change useable reserves, they indicate control gaps in capital asset management and accounting. For a large property-owning authority like City of London, accurate asset classification is material to understanding the composition and value of the estate.
findings.figures: £19.2m incorrectly classified at 31 March 2025; £13m reclassified to investment properties under development; £6.2m moved to intangible assets; £21.8m prior period adjustment to opening balance
findings.quote: Management had classified all AUC additions in the current year of £153.2m solely as property, plant and equipment. The closing balance of assets under construction classified as property, plant and equipment was £351.9m at 31 March 2025. While performing our audit procedures, we identified that some of the AUC assets included within the closing balance at year end should be classified as investment property under development or intangible assets.

findings.headline: Significant weakness identified: low Housing Revenue Account reserve balance threatens financial sustainability.
findings.detail: The auditor identified one significant weakness in value-for-money arrangements relating to the low HRA (Housing Revenue Account) Reserve balance. The auditor was generally satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for economy, efficiency and effectiveness, but flagged this reserve position as an area of concern.
findings.matters: HRA reserves fund housing maintenance and capital investment. A depleted reserve signals reduced capacity to absorb cost shocks, service pressures, or investment needs in social housing. Lenders assess reserve adequacy as a buffer against financial stress.

findings.paper_url: https://democracy.cityoflondon.gov.uk/documents/s223173/City of London Corporation - City Fund Audit Findings Report 2024-25.pdf
findings.headline: Pension liability understated by £90m due to IFRIC 14 accounting treatment not applied.
findings.detail: The Local Government Pension Scheme (LGPS) was in surplus for the first time, with assets exceeding liabilities. However, an asset ceiling under IFRIC 14 needed to be applied due to an assessed minimum funding requirement constituting an onerous funding commitment. The auditor found management had not incorporated this assessment into the accounts, understating the net pension liability at 31 March 2025. This required a material adjustment from £671.8m to £762.2m, with matching remeasurement adjustments.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are a major balance sheet item affecting net financial position and solvency. Lenders to councils assess sustainability partly through pension reserve positions. A £90m restatement indicates financial reporting control gaps at a significant scale.
findings.figures: Net pension liability increased by £90m from £671.8m to £762.2m; LGPS assets £715.9m, obligations £645.4m at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: While the management expert actuary assessed the impact of IFRIC 14 in relation to the LGPS scheme, our audit work identified that management did not incorporate this assessment into the preparation of the financial statements. This omission resulted in the recording of a surplus asset for the year which understated the City Fund's pension liability at 31 March 2025. The total understatement was £90.4 million.

findings.detail: Despite being flagged in the prior audit, the Fund has not implemented approval controls for journal entries under £100k. This has been identified as potentially affecting Local Government Pension Schemes. Management has classified this as a contingent liability and updated Note 19 disclosures.

findings.headline: Asset Management Strategy for HRA not yet finalised; risks emergency repair costs to already-vulnerable reserve
findings.detail: The Asset Management Strategy for the HRA, which should be fully costed with annual supporting plans and monitoring arrangements, is not yet developed or implemented. The auditor has raised an improvement recommendation to finalise this with priority, citing the vulnerable HRA reserve position. Without a full costed strategy, the council risks further emergency repair and maintenance costs—a historical pressure on the HRA.
findings.matters: The HRA reserve is already critically low. Unanticipated emergency repairs could push it into deficit. A full Asset Management Strategy is the backstop against this; its absence is flagged by the auditor as a material risk.
findings.figures: HRA reserve £0.034m; repairs and maintenance estimated at £0.212m less in 2025-26 than 2024-25 actual
findings.quote: A lack of fully costed Asset Management Strategy, as pertains to the HRA, could lead to unanticipated emergency repairs and maintenance costs in the medium-term, which have been a significant pressure on the HRA Reserve over several years.

findings.headline: Pension Fund pooling deadline at risk; only 56% of assets pooled by required date of 31 March 2026
findings.detail: The Pension Fund must pool 100% of assets by 31 March 2026 under government policy ('Fit for Future'). As at July 2025, only 56% are managed by pooled arrangements (London CIV or other pools), with 4% additional commitment outstanding. This is an increase from 36% in March 2024 but leaves a significant proportion to transfer in a short timeframe. A Pooling Transition Plan is planned but not yet formalised.
findings.matters: The deadline is statutory-backed but the legal and regulatory consequences of missing it are currently uncertain. The pace required to move 40% of assets in the remaining months poses operational risk.
findings.figures: 56% of investments pooled as at July 2025; 4% additional commitment outstanding; was 36% at 31 March 2024; deadline 31 March 2026
findings.quote: The Government published its 'Fit for Future' consultation response in May 2025. This confirmed that funds should have all their assets under pool management by 31 March 2026... As at July 2025 56% of investment are managed by the London CIV Pool, or other pooled management arrangements, with an additional outstanding 4% commitment to the LCIV Renewable Infrastructure Fund.

findings.headline: Capital programme has £150.9m slippage (33.8% of budget), no new projects solicited for 2025-26
findings.detail: The capital programme shows BAU slippage of £86.9m and major projects slippage of £64m. No new capital proposals were requested for 2025-26; the programme comprises only existing projects. This is supported by £7m contingency held from 2026-27 and a re-prioritisation process to ensure affordability without external borrowing. The council continues funding Cyclical Works and the Barbican renewal programme.
findings.matters: Large slippage suggests either optimism bias in planning, delivery challenges, or prudent restraint. The decision to reject new bids and rely only on existing projects suggests tightening capital discipline amid wider financial pressure.
findings.figures: Total capital slippage £150.9m (33.8% of 2024-25 budgeted programme); BAU £86.9m, major projects £64m; Barbican renewal total £307m over life; £7m contingency held
findings.quote: City Fund's capital programme, underpinned by the Capital Strategy, continues to be challenged. The BAU programme has slippage of £86.9m and the major projects programme has slippage of £64m, £150.9m overall or 33.8% of the budgeted capital programme for 2024-25.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan shows £59.3m deficit over 2026-27 to 2028-29; unidentified savings of £4.4m still needed
findings.detail: While the general fund achieved a £23.4m underspend in 2024-25 and built reserves to £283.4m, the MTFP projects a significant deficit from 2026-27 onwards. The council has £4.4m of unidentified savings across the planning period, with £2.8m needed in 2025-26. The council is responding by creating a new Transformation Programme supported by an external Strategic Partner, with governance arrangements already in place but implementation still to come.
findings.matters: A council that cannot identify recurring savings faces an eventual reserve drawdown or service cuts. The plan depends on identifying a Strategic Partner and delivering transformation rather than incremental savings, which is higher-risk.

findings.quote: the MTFP estimates that 2026-27 onwards, will fall into a deficit of £59.3m over the remaining 3 years of the MTFP. At this stage it is anticipated that the position may need to be managed through reserves; however, City Fund has built the reserves up over several years and the balances are adequate to support the position temporarily as alternative solutions are identified.

findings.headline: HRA reserves have collapsed to critical low, down from budgeted surplus to actual deficit
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account was budgeted for a £0.144m surplus but delivered a £0.275m deficit instead. This reduces reserves to £0.034m, leaving almost no buffer against unexpected costs. The position is now described as 'critical' by the auditor. The council's 10-year recovery plan depends on assumptions around rent-generating units that have underperformed historically.
findings.matters: An HRA with near-zero reserves cannot absorb volatility in repairs costs or income. Statutory law requires the HRA to remain in balance or surplus; this reserve position is at breaking point.
findings.figures: HRA Reserve balance £0.034m at end 2024-25; deficit of £0.275m in 2024-25 against planned surplus of £0.144m; repairs and maintenance expected to be £0.212m less than prior year but vulnerable to cost overruns
findings.quote: The HRA deficit of £0.275m for 2024-25, reduces the HRA Reserve balance to £0.034m. The position is extremely vulnerable to even small variances from assumptions made around variable and volatile line items within the budget. The current position of City Fund's HRA balance is considered critical.
